Seedtime
SEED-time
n. (the season of sowing)
Hebrew zera, seed or sowing, from zara, to scatter seed. The Authorized Version compounds it with time to render the season of sowing, first of the six pairs in God's promise after the flood.

Biblical Definition

While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease. The promise is given after the flood, and its form is worth noticing: six pairs, each a rhythm rather than a state. Seedtime with harvest, cold with heat, summer with winter, day with night. God does not promise uninterrupted mildness; he promises that the alternation will hold. The cold is guaranteed along with the heat, and the night along with the day. This is the foundation of what theologians call common grace — the ordinary reliability of the created order, extended to everyone without distinction. The Lord states the principle in his own words: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. Paul preached the same to pagans at Lystra, saying that God left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. Two things follow. All settled agriculture, science, and ordinary planning rest on a promise God made to Noah, whether or not the planners know it. And the promise has a stated limit: while the earth remaineth. The seasons are guaranteed until the end, not for ever, and Peter builds a warning on exactly that reservation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the season proper for sowing; the season of sowing seed.

expand to see more

SEED-TIME, n. The season proper for sowing.

SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species.

HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.

SEASON, n. One of the four divisions of the year, spring, summer, autumn, winter; a fit or suitable time.

COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; in theology, God's promise and engagement.

Key Scripture

Genesis 8:22 — "While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease."

Genesis 9:11 — "And I will establish my covenant with you; neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters of a flood; neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth."

Matthew 5:45 — "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust."

Acts 14:17 — "Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness."

Modern Corruption

The regularity of nature is taken as a self-explaining property of a closed system; Scripture presents it as a covenant promise, freely given, and expressly bounded by the end of the age.

expand to see more

The uniformity of nature is the working assumption of every science and of all ordinary life, and it is generally treated as a brute fact needing no explanation — things have always gone on this way, therefore they will. Genesis 8:22 gives the ground of it, and the ground is personal: God said this would hold. That does not make the study of nature suspect; it makes it possible, and the Christian doctrine of creation is a large part of why the natural sciences arose where they did. What it denies is that the regularity is self-sustaining. The seasons are kept by a promise, not by the universe's own resources.

Peter takes up this exact point and turns it into a warning. He describes scoffers who say, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation — an argument from uniformity against the return of Christ. His answer is that they willingly forget the flood, the one occasion when the ordinary course did not continue, and the reservation written into the promise itself: while the earth remaineth. The rhythms are guaranteed until the end and not past it. A man who builds on the permanence of seedtime and harvest has read half the sentence.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zera (H2233), seed, sowing; qatsir (H7105), harvest; qor (H7120), cold; berith (H1285), covenant.

expand to see more

Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed, sowing; the first term of the first pair.

Hebrew qatsir (H7105) — harvest, the reaping season; paired with seedtime.

Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to rest; shall not cease.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; established with Noah and every living creature.

Hebrew owd (H5750) — again, any more; neither shall there any more be a flood.

Usage

"“seedtime and harvest” — the first of six guaranteed rhythms."

"“cold and heat” — the hard half promised with the pleasant."

"“while the earth remaineth” — the limit written into the promise."
